papers.title: Emotion beyond boundaries: How multimodal cues foster cross-cultural affective contagion in immersive livestreaming
papers.authors: Yu Zhang, Yuanyuan Liu, Haoran Mao, and Junxiang Zhao
papers.category: 甲亢哥访华 · direct IShowSpeed China-tour evidence
papers.evidence: Publisher or authoritative index record verified
papers.takeaway: Using Bilibili material surrounding IShowSpeed’s China tour, this study combines network analysis, sentiment analysis, and epidemiological modeling to examine cross-cultural emotional diffusion in immersive livestreaming. It finds decentralized, algorithmically amplified circulation, a prominent role for high-arousal positive emotion, and contagion patterns associated with emotional similarity. The evidence is directly tied to the China tour and helps explain how creator affect can spread across cultural boundaries, although it does not by itself establish durable changes in national image or attitudes toward China.

papers.title: “Oh my god! bro, is this really China?!” Telling the “China story” through digital storytelling: a case study of IShowSpeed’s China tour
papers.category: 甲亢哥访华 · direct IShowSpeed China-tour evidence
papers.evidence: Publisher or authoritative index record verified
papers.takeaway: This mixed-methods case study analyzes IShowSpeed’s China tour as digital storytelling. It describes a combination of narrative reconstruction, emotional co-presence, multimodal presentation, and networked diffusion that turns travel livestreaming into a highly visible account of contemporary China. The study argues that the tour stimulated cultural curiosity and provided concrete, experience-based images of China, while warning that spectacle and compressed cultural explanation can flatten complexity. The article is retained for direct relevance despite its lower indexing tier.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence adoption and employee well-being: A job demands-resources perspective from academia and practice (scoping review)
papers.authors: Carel Chan, Stephen Tan, Antonia Girardi, and Dominic Gasbarro
papers.category: Workplace AI and well-being · direct scoping review
papers.evidence: Publisher or authoritative index record verified
papers.takeaway: This scoping review synthesizes 48 sources published from 2019 to 2025, including 35 academic studies and 13 practitioner reports, through a Job Demands–Resources lens. Existing work emphasizes stress and burnout more than engagement and gives limited attention to personal resources, work design, and job crafting. The review treats AI-enabled work as an ambivalent characteristic that can create demands and resources simultaneously and identifies job crafting as a promising way for employees to rebalance them. It offers a direct map of workplace AI and well-being evidence rather than a causal estimate from a single workforce.

papers.title: Optimizing AI adoption through HR practices: Systematic review and theoretical framework for improved employee well-being
papers.authors: Sitong Yu, Shota Kawasaki, Federico Magni, Kang Yang Trevor Yu, and Vijayan P. Munusamy
papers.category: Workplace AI and well-being · direct systematic review
papers.evidence: Publisher or authoritative index record verified
papers.takeaway: This systematic review synthesizes 74 articles on how workplace AI adoption relates to employees’ psychological, social, and physical well-being. It finds that AI presents both opportunities and challenges and that outcomes depend on how employees appraise and evaluate the technology. Drawing on the ability–motivation–opportunity model, the authors organize HR practices that can build employees’ capabilities, motivation, and opportunities to use AI while protecting well-being. The article directly addresses organizational conditions under which AI may improve or diminish well-being, but its framework integrates prior studies rather than testing one intervention.

toc.title: Communication and constitution: exploring classical and emerging topics relationally
toc.abstractEn: This special-issue introduction treats communication as constitutive and relational rather than merely transmissive. It connects the issue’s articles through a relational ontology in which social forms emerge, endure, and transform through communicative events involving both humans and other-than-human actors.

toc.title: Expression and reality: a dialogue on communication, constitution, and process philosophy
toc.authors: Brian Massumi and Boris H. J. M. Brummans
toc.abstractEn: Presented as a theoretical dialogue, this article uses process philosophy to reconsider how communication participates in the constitution of collectives and reality. Communication is approached as expression and event, opening conceptual alternatives to models that begin with stable entities and then add relations between them.

toc.title: How are worlds communicatively constituted?
toc.abstractEn: This theoretical article explains how recurring everyday interaction in small-scale social worlds contributes to the constitution of larger social worlds. Repeated practices and meanings generate emergent interpretive properties through which groups become recognizable and durable.

toc.title: Hybrid stakeholders and processes in social impact organizing: a constitutive approach to hybridity
toc.authors: Jiawei Sophia Fu and Katherine R. Cooper
toc.abstractEn: The article develops a constitutive view of hybridity in social-impact organizing. It argues that hybrid stakeholders and hybrid processes do not merely inhabit pre-existing organizational arrangements but help communicatively construct the social reality in which impact organizing occurs.

toc.title: Statues and culture wars. How statues communicatively constitute organizational cultures in conflictual situations
toc.abstractEn: Using the Oxford Rhodes statue controversy and the Montreal School concept of ventriloquism, this article analyzes how statues are made to speak and act in organizational culture conflicts. It shows how material objects can be mobilized to impose or resist competing cultural narratives.

toc.title: Communication skills as generic objects: a relational view
toc.abstractEn: Drawing on public-speaking cases from the United States and China, this article asks how communication skills materialize relationally as generic objects. It argues that resources become desirable skills through their connections to valued ends and through narratives of personal transformation.

toc.title: Communicative relationality meets Deleuzian techniques and forces: materializations of power in communicatively constituting a fluid social movement
toc.abstractEn: Based on interviews, observation, and social-media material from the Stop Cop City movement, this article traces how power materializes through multimodal links among activists and state actors. It extends a techniques-and-forces approach with the concept of substantiating and examines identity, geography, time, and civic relations in a fluid movement.

toc.title: An articulation of the aesthetic tradition of communication theory for the future of Performance Studies in Communication
toc.abstractEn: This theoretical article proposes an Aesthetic Tradition as an extension of Craig’s metamodel of communication theory. Reviewing nearly four decades of scholarship, it shows how the tradition can organize work in public speaking, interpersonal and family communication, organizational communication, and arts-based research.

papers.title: Intercultural circulation of canonical literature facilitated by popularizing translation: a case study of Julia Lovell’s English translation of Xi You Ji
papers.category: Dissertation · direct Chinese-myth translation and circulation
papers.evidence: Publisher or authoritative index record verified
papers.takeaway: This study uses close textual and paratextual analysis of Julia Lovell’s English Monkey King: Journey to the West to explain how popularizing translation broadens the circulation of canonical literature. It identifies transcreation through prose adaptation of poetry, recontextualized humor, generalized cultural differences, narrative condensation, and globally recognizable visual and audio elements. The evidence concerns how an Anglophone-facing version reduces specialized cultural knowledge demands and frames the Monkey King for international readers; it analyzes translation strategy and circulation rather than measuring audience attitudes experimentally.

papers.title: A Meta-Analysis Examining the Role of Character-Recipient Similarity in Narrative Persuasion
papers.authors: Meng Chen, Yujie Dong, and Jilong Wang
papers.evidence: Publisher or authoritative index record verified
papers.takeaway: This meta-analysis synthesizes 123 effects from 19 articles on similarity between narrative characters and recipients. Character similarity produces small but significant increases in identification and self-referencing, while effects on transportation and resistance are marginal. Effects are stronger when similarity is deliberately selected rather than incidental and vary with demographic or biographical similarity, first-person perspective, and social-issue context. This is adjacent mechanism evidence rather than a study of Chinese mythology, but it directly informs whether audience-character congruence can move reception beyond liking toward identification.
